# Reading 1: Introduction to Jupyter Notebook Interface


### What is it?

**Jupyter Notebook** is a tool that runs in your web browser. You write a few lines of Python in a box called a **cell**, press **Shift + Enter**, and the answer appears straight below. Then you write the next cell. Step by step, your notebook becomes a record of what you tried and what you found.

The name comes from three programming languages it was first built for: Julia, Python and R. Notebooks are saved as **.ipynb** files. One file holds your code, its outputs and your notes together, so someone else can open it and follow your thinking. Notebooks are widely used in data science, machine learning, research and teaching. Free online services such as Google Colab and Kaggle use the same notebook format, so what you learn here works there too.

Before installing Jupyter, the tutorial creates a **virtual environment**. Think of it as a separate cupboard for one project. Everything you install for this course goes into that cupboard and does not disturb the rest of your computer. If something goes wrong, you can delete the cupboard and start again.


### Commands at a glance


| **Type this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| python3 --version | Checks that Python is installed and shows its version |
| python3 -m venv myenv | Creates a virtual environment named myenv |
| source myenv/bin/activate | Switches the environment on; (myenv) appears before the prompt |
| pip install notebook | Installs Jupyter Notebook inside the environment |
| jupyter notebook | Starts Jupyter and opens its home page in the browser |
| Shift + Enter (in a cell) | Runs the cell and shows the output below it |
| Ctrl + S (in a notebook) | Saves the notebook |

Each time you come back to the course, open the terminal, run the source command again, and then run jupyter notebook. If (myenv) is missing from the prompt, the environment is not switched on.


### A real-world example

Priya is a second-year B.Com student in Nagpur. Her teacher asks the class to work out the average of their monthly phone bills. Priya has always done such sums on a calculator, line by line, and loses track when she makes a mistake. This time she opens a notebook. In the first cell she types the six bills, in the second she adds them up, and in the third she divides by six. When she spots a wrong figure, she corrects only the first cell and runs the rest again. Her working is all on one page, and she can show it to her teacher.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| python3 -m venv shows an error about ensurepip or venv | The venv package is not installed on Ubuntu | Run sudo apt install python3-venv, then try again |
| jupyter: command not found | The virtual environment is not switched on | Run source myenv/bin/activate, check that (myenv) appears, then run jupyter notebook again |
| Pressing Enter in a cell adds a new line instead of running it | Enter alone starts a new line | Press Shift + Enter to run the cell |
| The browser does not open | Some systems do not open it automatically | Copy the link starting with http://localhost:8888 from the terminal into the browser |

# Reading 2: Installing Libraries inside Jupyter Notebook


### What is it?

A **library** is ready-made code that someone else has written and shared. Instead of writing your own code to draw a graph or handle a table, you install a library and use it. Python has thousands of free libraries. Nobody builds AI from scratch: even large AI systems are built on libraries like these.

Using a library takes two steps. First you **install** it once, with pip. In a notebook cell you type !pip install numpy. The ! sign tells Jupyter to send that line to the system, as if you had typed it in the terminal. Then you **import** it in each notebook where you want to use it. Installing puts the library on your computer. Importing brings it into your notebook.


### Libraries at a glance


| **Library** | **What it is for** | **Install** | **Import** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NumPy | Fast calculations on lists of numbers (arrays) | !pip install numpy | import numpy as np |
| Pandas | Working with tables of data | !pip install pandas | import pandas as pd |
| Matplotlib | Drawing graphs and charts | !pip install matplotlib | import matplotlib.pyplot as plt |
| Seaborn | Attractive statistical charts, built on Matplotlib | !pip install seaborn | import seaborn as sns |

The short names np, pd, plt and sns are a habit almost everyone follows. You will see them in books, courses and code online, so it helps to use them too.


### A real-world example

Imran runs a small mobile repair shop in Lucknow and is learning Python in the evenings. He wants to see which phone brands come in most often for repair, and a friend tells him to "use Pandas". He types import pandas as pd and gets ModuleNotFoundError. He thinks he has broken something. Then he reads the message again: it simply says Pandas is not there yet. He runs !pip install pandas, waits for it to finish, and runs the import again. No error this time. He makes a small table of five repairs to check that it works.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas' | The library is not installed in this environment | Run !pip install pandas, then run the import again |
| ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandaas' | The name is spelt wrongly | Read the name in the error carefully and fix the spelling |
| NameError: name 'pd' is not defined | The library is installed but not imported in this notebook | Run import pandas as pd first |
| The library installs, but the import still fails | Jupyter was started from a different environment | Close Jupyter, activate the right environment, start Jupyter again |

tutorial_contents.reading_markdown:
# Reading 3: Managing Notebook Kernels and Runtimes


### What is it?

When you run a cell, the notebook page does not run the code itself. It sends the code to a program working in the background called the **kernel**. The kernel runs the code, sends back the result and remembers every variable you have created. This memory lasts as long as the kernel is running.

That is why a variable created in one cell can be printed in a later cell without typing it again. The kernel is holding it in memory.

After a restart, your cells and outputs are still on the page, but the kernel has forgotten everything. If you print a variable now, you get **NameError**, because Python cannot find it. To get it back, run the cell that created it again.

Before you call a notebook finished, use **Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells**. This checks that the notebook works from top to bottom on a clean start. A notebook that only works because of a cell you ran earlier and later deleted will confuse anyone who opens it next, including you.


### Kernel actions at a glance


| **Do this** | **What it does** | **Your variables** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kernel → Interrupt Kernel | Stops the cell that is running now, such as a loop that never ends | Kept |
| Kernel → Restart Kernel | Stops everything and starts a fresh kernel | Cleared |
| Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells | Starts fresh and runs every cell from the top | Rebuilt from your code |
| File → Close and Shut Down Notebook | Closes the notebook and stops its kernel | Cleared |

The number in square brackets next to a cell, such as [7], shows the order in which the cells were run. A [*] means the cell is still running.


### A real-world example

Lakshmi is preparing marks for her class project. She loads the data, cleans it over many cells and gets a neat result. Then she deletes a messy cell she no longer needs. The next morning she reopens the notebook, runs it and gets NameError halfway down. The deleted cell had created a variable that later cells needed. Yesterday it still lived in the kernel's memory, so she never noticed. Now, before calling a notebook finished, she always restarts the kernel and runs all cells.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NameError after a restart, for a variable that worked before | Restarting cleared the kernel's memory | Run the cell that creates the variable, or Restart and Run All |
| A cell shows [*] and never finishes | The code is stuck, for example in a loop that never ends | Kernel → Interrupt Kernel, then fix the code |
| The notebook works for you but not for a classmate | It depends on a cell you ran earlier and then deleted or changed | Restart and Run All before sharing, and fix any cell that fails |
| Restarting lost data that took long to load | Restart was used when Interrupt was enough | Use Interrupt to stop a cell; use Restart only when you want a clean start |

# Reading 4: Working with Notebook Markdown Documentation


### What is it?

A notebook has two main kinds of cells. Code cells hold Python. **Markdown cells** hold plain text that explains your work. Every new cell starts as a code cell, so you change it to Markdown from the cell type drop-down at the top of the notebook. Press **Shift + Enter**, and the text is shown neatly formatted. To change a Markdown cell after it is shown, double-click it.

Code tells the computer what to do. It does not tell a person why. A short line above each block of code, such as "Remove rows with missing marks", makes the notebook easy to read, check and share. A good pattern is: a title at the top, a short description of the goal, then a Markdown cell before each step that says what the next code does.


### Markdown at a glance


| **Type this in a Markdown cell** | **You get** |
| --- | --- |
| # My Project | A large heading (level 1) |
| ## Data | A smaller heading (level 2) |
| - Apples | A bullet point |
| 1. First step | A numbered point |
| **Important** | Bold text |
| *note* | Italic text |


### A real-world example

Vikram, a final-year engineering student in Coimbatore, shares his project notebook with his guide. It has forty code cells and no text. His guide replies: "I can see the code runs, but I can't tell what each part is for." Vikram adds a heading at the top, a two-line description of the problem, and a short note before each group of cells, such as "Step 3: Draw the monthly sales graph". He puts the main finding in bold at the end. His guide now reads it in ten minutes and suggests one change.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| # My Title shows nothing, or no heading appears | The cell is still a code cell, so # starts a comment | Change the cell type to Markdown, then press Shift + Enter |
| The symbols ## or ** show as plain text | The cell has not been run yet | Press Shift + Enter to show the formatted text |
| #Heading does not become a heading | There is no space after # | Type a space: # Heading |
| The next new cell is a code cell again | Every new cell starts as code | Change the type to Markdown each time you need text |

# Reading 5: Loading CSV Datasets


### What is it?

A **dataset** is a collection of related information, usually set out as a table. Each **row** is one record, such as one student. Each **column** is one piece of information about every record, such as Name or Marks. AI models learn from data, so loading and checking a dataset is the first step of almost every AI project.

A **CSV file** (comma-separated values) is the simplest way to store such a table. It is plain text. The first line holds the column names, and each line after that is one row, with commas between the values:


```python
Name,Age,Marks,City
Anita,19,82,Pune
Faisal,20,74,Bhopal
```

You can open a CSV file in a spreadsheet, a text editor or Python. In Pandas, a few commands give you a first look at it. Pandas stores the table as a **DataFrame**.


### Commands at a glance


| **Type this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| import pandas as pd | Brings Pandas into the notebook |
| data = pd.read_csv("students.csv") | Loads the file into a DataFrame called data |
| data.head() | Shows the first five rows; data.head(10) shows ten |
| data.shape | Shows the size as (rows, columns), for example (5, 4) |
| data.columns | Shows the column names |
| data.info() | Shows the column names, their types and how many values are filled in |

These first checks catch problems early: a file with only half the rows, a missing column, or marks stored as text. CSV is also one of the most common formats for sharing public data, including many datasets from Indian government departments.


### A real-world example

Sunita teaches Class 10 at a government school near Jaipur. The district office sends her a CSV file of her students' test results. In a spreadsheet she scrolls and scrolls and is not sure how many students are in it. In a notebook, she loads it with read_csv and runs data.shape. The answer is (38, 6): 38 students and 6 columns. But she has 42 students. She checks data.head() to see the format, then emails the office with the exact number missing, before anyone makes a report from incomplete data.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FileNotFoundError: No such file or directory | The CSV file is not in the notebook's folder, or the name is spelt differently | Move the file into the same folder as the notebook, and check the name and capital letters |
| NameError: name 'pd' is not defined | Pandas was not imported | Run import pandas as pd first |
| TypeError: 'tuple' object is not callable | You typed data.shape() with brackets | shape has no brackets: data.shape |
| All the data appears in one column | The file uses another separator, such as ; | Use pd.read_csv("file.csv", sep=";") |

# Reading 6: Creating Visual Graphs


### What is it?

**Data visualisation** means showing data as a picture, such as a graph or chart. A column of fifty numbers is hard to read. The same numbers as a line going up or down can be understood in a second. A sudden spike, or a value far away from the others, jumps out in a picture but hides in a table. Graphs are also how results are shown to people who will never read the code.

In the tutorial you drew a line graph with Matplotlib:


```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
y = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.show()
```

The **x-axis** (horizontal) usually shows what changes on its own, such as months. The **y-axis** (vertical) shows what you measure, such as sales. plot() joins the points in the order given, and show() displays the graph below the cell. The x and y lists must have the same number of values.


### Commands at a glance


| **Type this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| plt.plot(x, y) | Draws a line graph: good for values that change over time |
| plt.bar(x, y) | Draws a bar chart: good for comparing groups |
| plt.scatter(x, y) | Draws a scatter plot: good for seeing how two measures relate |
| plt.title("Monthly sales") | Adds a title above the graph |
| plt.xlabel("Month") and plt.ylabel("Sales (Rs)") | Labels the axes, including units |
| plt.show() | Shows the graph below the cell |
| plt.savefig("sales.png") | Saves the graph as an image file (put it before plt.show()) |


### A real-world example

Ramesh grows tomatoes near Kolar and sells them at the mandi. His daughter, a BCA student, types in the price he got each week for twelve weeks and plots it. The line shows something neither of them had noticed: prices dropped every time a festival week ended, then rose again within two weeks. With a title and labelled axes, she shows the graph to her father on her phone. He decides to hold back part of his harvest after the next festival instead of selling it all at once.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ValueError: x and y must have same first dimension | The x and y lists have different numbers of values | Make both lists the same length |
| The graph has no title or labels, and readers ask what it shows | Title and labels were not added | Add plt.title(), plt.xlabel() and plt.ylabel() |

# Reading 7: Interactive Experimentation


### What is it?

Interactive experimentation means changing one thing, running the cell again and seeing what happens. In the tutorial, a variable was set to 5, then changed to 100, then to 25. Each time the cell was run, the output changed straight away. Storing a new value in a variable that already exists is called **reassignment**. The old value is replaced.

Much of AI work is experimentation: what happens with more data, a different setting or a different model? Changing only one thing at a time, and noting what happened, is how you learn which change made the difference.

Three facts explain how this works in a notebook:

1. **A cell runs only when you run it.** Changing the code does nothing until you press Shift + Enter.
2. **The kernel keeps the latest value.** Whatever value was stored last is the one later cells use, until you change it again or restart the kernel.
3. **The order of running matters, not the order on the page.** The number in square brackets next to a cell, such as [7], shows when it was last run.
Python also lets one variable hold different kinds of values. age = 25 holds a whole number (**int**). age = "Student" holds text (**str**). age = 25.5 holds a decimal number (**float**).


### Code at a glance


| **Type this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| marks = 85 | Creates a variable named marks with the value 85 |
| marks = 90 | Reassigns marks; the old value 85 is replaced |
| marks | On the last line of a cell, shows the value of marks |
| print(marks) | Prints the value of marks from anywhere in a cell |
| type(marks) | Shows the kind of value: int, float or str |


### A real-world example

Anjali is planning to save for a laptop that costs Rs 45,000. In a notebook she writes monthly_saving = 3000 and a cell that divides the price by it. The answer is 15 months. That feels too long, so she tries 4000 and runs the cell again: just over 11 months. Then 5000: 9 months. In two minutes she has tried three plans without writing three programs. She settles on Rs 4,500 a month and writes her choice in a Markdown cell so she remembers why.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The output did not change after you edited the code | The edited cell was not run | Press Shift + Enter on the edited cell |
| A later cell uses an old value | You changed a value but did not rerun the cells after it | Rerun the cells below, or use Restart and Run All |
| The result looks wrong although the code looks right | Cells were run out of order | Check the numbers in [ ], then Restart and Run All |
| TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str | Text and a number were added together | Use the same type, for example str(age) or int(text) |

# Reading 8: Debugging Notebook Workflows


### What is it?

A bug is a mistake in code. **Debugging** is finding and fixing it. Every programmer, from a beginner to an expert, spends a large part of their time debugging. An error message is not a sign that you are bad at coding. It is Python telling you exactly where it got stuck.

An error message has three useful parts. Read them from the bottom up:

1. **The error type** on the last line, such as SyntaxError or NameError.
2. **A short description** after the type, such as '(' was never closed.
3. **The line number**, and often a ^ mark pointing near the problem.
Python stops at the first error it finds. Fix it, rerun the cell, and the next error, if there is one, will show. If you are stuck, copy the last line of the error into a search engine or an AI chatbot. Thousands of people have seen it before.


### Errors at a glance


| **Error** | **What it means** | **Common cause** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SyntaxError | The code does not follow Python's rules, so nothing runs | A missing bracket, quote or colon |
| NameError | Python cannot find a variable or function with that name | A typo, or the cell that creates it was not run |
| ModuleNotFoundError | Python cannot find a library | Not installed, or a different environment |
| IndentationError | The spaces at the start of a line are wrong | Lines inside a loop or function not indented the same way |
| TypeError | An operation was used on the wrong kind of value | Adding text and a number |
| ValueError | The value is the right type but cannot be used | int("eighty") |


### A real-world example

Dinesh, a polytechnic student in Hubli, types print("Total marks" and runs the cell. A red block appears. His first thought is to delete the cell and start again. Instead, he reads the last line: SyntaxError: '(' was never closed. The ^ mark points at the opening bracket. He adds the closing bracket, runs the cell again, and it works. It takes ten seconds.


### Common mistakes when debugging


| **What you do** | **Why it does not help** | **Do this instead** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delete the cell and retype everything | You may make the same mistake again and learn nothing | Read the last line of the error first |
| Change several things at once | You cannot tell which change fixed it, or broke something else | Fix one error, rerun, check, then move on |
| Read only the top of the message | The error type and description are at the bottom | Read the error message from the bottom up |
| Ignore the line number | You search the whole cell for the problem | Go straight to the line the message points to |

# Reading 9: Running Basic Learning Workflows


### What is it?

**Machine learning** is a way of teaching a computer to find patterns in examples, so that it can make a guess about new cases. Instead of writing rules by hand, you show it many examples with the right answers, and it learns the rules itself.

Every machine learning project follows the same broad steps, called a **workflow**:

1. **Load** the data.
2. **Explore** it: look at its size, columns and values.
3. **Prepare** it: clean it and split it into a part for learning and a part for testing.
4. **Train** a model on the learning part.
5. **Evaluate** the model on the testing part to see how often it is right.
This tutorial covers steps 1 and 2 with a famous practice dataset, the **Iris dataset**. It holds measurements of 150 iris flowers from three species: setosa, versicolor and virginica. For each flower there are four measurements, in centimetres: sepal length, sepal width, petal length and petal width. In machine learning, the inputs are called **features** and the answer to be predicted is called the **target** (or label).

The Iris dataset comes built into **Scikit-learn**, a free Python library with machine learning tools and sample datasets. The same workflow is used for real problems, such as predicting crop disease or spotting fraud in bank transactions. Only the data and the model change.


### Code at a glance


| **Type this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| !pip install scikit-learn | Installs Scikit-learn, if it is not already installed |
| from sklearn.datasets import load_iris | Brings in the function that loads the Iris dataset |
| data = load_iris() | Loads the dataset into data |
| data.data[:5] | Shows the measurements (features) of the first five flowers |
| data.data.shape | Shows the size: (150, 4) |
| data.target[:5] | Shows the species (target) of the first five flowers, as 0, 1 or 2 |
| data.feature_names and data.target_names | Show the names of the four measurements and the three species |

[:5] means "the first five". [:3] would mean the first three.


### A real-world example

Meera's aunt runs a small flower nursery in Ooty. She can tell her plants apart at a glance, but a new helper cannot. Meera, a B.Sc. Computer Science student, wonders if a computer could learn to do it from simple measurements, the way the Iris dataset does. She records the petal length and width of twenty plants of each kind in a CSV file, with the plant name in the last column. Before thinking about any model, she loads it and checks the first rows, the shape and the three names in the target column. She now has features and a target, just like Iris.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sklearn' | Scikit-learn is not installed | Run !pip install scikit-learn, then import again |
| You type import scikit-learn and get a SyntaxError | The install name and the import name are different | Install as scikit-learn, but import from sklearn |
| data.shape gives an error | data is not a table; the measurements are inside data.data | Use data.data.shape |
| The target shows 0, 1 and 2 instead of names | The species are stored as numbers | Use data.target_names to see what each number means |

# Reading 10: Organising Notebook Projects


### What is it?

After a few weeks, most learners have a Desktop full of files named Untitled3.ipynb, data_final.csv and data_final2.csv. Finding anything takes longer than doing the work. Organising a project means giving each kind of file its own place and each file a clear name, from the start. A clear layout means you, a teammate or a teacher can open the project months later and understand it. It also matters in Module 4, where Git tracks whole project folders.

A simple layout that works for most AI and data projects:


```python
marks_analysis/
    notebooks/     your .ipynb files
    datasets/      the CSV files and other raw data
    images/        graphs you save
    outputs/       results and exported PDF or HTML files
    models/        trained models (later in your learning)
```

Use lower-case letters, underscores instead of spaces, and numbers at the start when files follow an order: 01_load_data.ipynb, not Untitled5.ipynb. Never edit the original raw data file; save cleaned data as a new file.

Exporting a notebook to PDF or HTML lets people who do not use Jupyter read your work, code and graphs included.


### Commands at a glance


| **Type this or do this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| mkdir marks_analysis | Creates a folder named marks_analysis |
| cd marks_analysis | Moves into that folder |
| mkdir notebooks datasets images outputs models | Creates five folders at once |
| ls | Lists what is in the current folder |
| File → Save and Export Notebook As → HTML or PDF | Saves a copy of the notebook as a web page or PDF |


### A real-world example

Harpreet, an MBA student in Amritsar, is asked by her professor for the notebook behind her market survey project. She finds four versions on her laptop and is not sure which is the latest. She sends the wrong one. For her next project she makes the five folders on day one. Raw survey data goes into datasets and is never edited. Every notebook name starts with a number. When the professor asks again, she sends a PDF from outputs within a minute.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Export to PDF fails with an error | PDF export needs extra software that most computers do not have | Export as HTML, open the HTML file in your browser, press Ctrl + P and choose Save as PDF |
| FileNotFoundError after moving the notebook into notebooks/ | The CSV path is now different | Use the path from the notebook to the file, for example ../datasets/marks.csv |
| Two files both called final.csv in different folders | Names say nothing about the contents | Use names that describe the file, such as marks_2026_term1.csv |
| Cleaned data overwrote the original | The cleaned table was saved with the same name | Keep raw files unchanged; save cleaned data under a new name |

# Reading 11: Introduction of VS Code on Ubuntu


### What is it?

**Visual Studio Code**, usually called VS Code, is a free, open source code editor made by Microsoft. It starts quickly, like a simple text editor, but it can also run, test and debug programs, like a full development environment. It works on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS, and is one of the most widely used code editors in the world.

When an AI project grows from a notebook into a real program with several files, people move to an editor like VS Code. It colours your code so it is easier to read, marks mistakes as you type, and lets you run, debug and track your project in one place. VS Code can also open Jupyter notebooks.

On Ubuntu, you download VS Code from code.visualstudio.com. Choose **Download for Linux (.deb)**, because Ubuntu installs .deb packages. Then install it from the terminal. sudo runs the command as administrator, so Ubuntu asks for your password. Press **Tab** after typing code_ and the terminal completes the long file name for you.


### Steps at a glance


| **Do this** | **What happens** |
| --- | --- |
| Download for Linux (.deb) from code.visualstudio.com | Saves the installer to your Downloads folder |
| cd Downloads, then ls | Moves into Downloads and shows the file, such as code_1.134.0-..._amd64.deb |
| sudo dpkg -i code_<version>_amd64.deb | Installs VS Code |
| Open VS Code from Show Apps | Opens the Welcome page |
| Ctrl + Shift + P, type color, choose Preferences: Color Theme | Changes the theme, for example to Light Modern |
| File → New Text File, then Ctrl + Shift + S | Creates a file and saves it with a name you choose |


### The main parts of the window


| **Part** | **Where it is** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Activity Bar | Far left column of icons | Switches between Explorer, Search, Source Control, Run and Debug, and Extensions |
| Explorer | Panel next to the Activity Bar | Shows the files and folders you have open |
| Editor | Centre | Where you open and edit files, each in its own tab |
| Status Bar | Bottom strip | Shows the line number, the file type and, for Python, the interpreter |


### A real-world example

Salim works at a cyber café in Malappuram and wants to learn programming. He has been writing Python in the default text editor, where everything is the same colour and he only finds out about a missing bracket when the program fails. He installs VS Code. The first time he opens a Python file, the keywords appear in different colours and a wavy red line shows under a missing bracket before he even runs it. He changes the theme to light through the Command Palette, because the café is bright.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dpkg: error: cannot access archive | You are not in the Downloads folder, or the file name is wrong | Run cd Downloads and ls, then type code_ and press Tab to complete the name |
| dpkg: error: requested operation requires superuser privilege | sudo was left out | Put sudo before the command |
| You downloaded an .exe or .rpm file | The wrong download button was clicked | Download the .deb file for Ubuntu |
| A window asks you to sign in | VS Code offers to sync settings | You can close it; signing in is not needed for this course |

# Reading 12: Working with Files and Folders


### What is it?

VS Code works best when you open a whole **folder**, not just a single file. The folder is your project. Everything inside it shows in the Explorer, and VS Code treats the files as belonging together. A real AI project is never one file: it has code, data, notebooks and a README. Working with a folder lets you see the whole project at a glance and search across all of it.

The first time you open a folder, VS Code asks whether you trust the authors of the files. For your own folders, click **Yes, I trust the authors**. For files downloaded from unknown places, choose the restricted option, because some files can run code when a folder is trusted.

The **file extension**, the part after the dot, tells VS Code which language a file is in. It uses this to colour the code and offer the right help. In the tutorial, three web files were created: index.html (the structure of a page), style.css (its look) and script.js (what happens when you click). A Python file ends in .py and a notebook in .ipynb.

Files created in VS Code are real files on your computer. Open the folder in the Files app and you will see them there. Deleted files go to the Trash, so you can get them back.


### Steps at a glance


| **Do this** | **What happens** |
| --- | --- |
| File → Open Folder, then choose the folder | Opens the folder as your project; its files show in the Explorer |
| Click Yes, I trust the authors | Allows all features for your own folder |
| Hover on the folder name in the Explorer, click New File | Creates a file; type its name with the extension and press Enter |
| Hover on the folder name, click New Folder | Creates a folder inside the project |
| Right-click a file → Rename | Changes the file name |
| Right-click a file → Delete → Move to Trash | Deletes the file; it can be restored from the Trash |


### A real-world example

Rekha runs a home tuition centre in Thrissur and is building a simple web page for it with help from her nephew. At first she opens each file separately and keeps losing track of which one she was editing. Her nephew shows her File → Open Folder. Now all the files sit in the Explorer. She renames test.html to fees.html so its purpose is clear, and deletes an old copy she no longer needs.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The Explorer is empty | A single file was opened, not the folder | Use File → Open Folder |
| The file has no colours and no Python help | The file has no extension, or the wrong one | Rename it with the right extension, such as marks.py |
| The new file was created in the wrong place | A different folder was selected in the Explorer | Click the right folder first, or drag the file into it |
| Some features are turned off and the window says Restricted Mode | The folder was opened without trusting it | For your own folder, click Manage in the banner and trust it |

# Reading 13: Integrated Terminal and Extensions


### What is it?

The **integrated terminal** is a normal Ubuntu terminal that opens inside the VS Code window, at the bottom. It starts in your project folder, so you can run commands on your files without switching windows. A folder you make in the terminal appears in the Explorer straight away, because both show the same folder on your computer.

**Extensions** are add-ons that give VS Code new abilities. You find them with the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar. Anyone can publish an extension, and an extension can read your files. Before installing, check the publisher's name, look for a verified badge, and prefer extensions with many downloads and recent updates.

A senior colleague shows him the integrated terminal. It opens already in the project folder. He types ls to check where he is, then mkdir data, and sees the folder appear in the Explorer at once. Then he installs the Python extension, checking that the publisher is Microsoft, and closes the other two windows.

# Reading 14: Python Development Workflow


### What is it?

In a notebook, you run code one cell at a time. A **.py file** is different: it is a complete program that runs from the first line to the last every time. Most software, including AI applications, is made of .py files.

The **interpreter** is the program that reads and runs your Python code. Its version, such as Python 3.12, is shown in the Status Bar at the bottom of VS Code. Click it to choose a different one, for example the Python inside a virtual environment. This matters because libraries installed in one environment are not visible to another.

The tutorial's Student Marks Calculator:


```python
name = input("Enter student name: ")
m1 = int(input("Enter English marks: "))
m2 = int(input("Enter Maths marks: "))
m3 = int(input("Enter Science marks: "))
total = m1 + m2 + m3
average = total / 3
print("Student:", name)
print("Total:", total)
print("Average:", average)
```

**input()** waits for the user to type something and press Enter. Whatever is typed comes in as text. **int()** turns that text into a whole number so it can be added. Without int(), "80" + "75" would join the text to make "8075" instead of adding to 155.

Always test a program with values whose answer you already know. In the tutorial, 80, 75 and 85 gave a total of 240 and an average of 80.0, which you can check in your head.


### Steps at a glance


| **Do this** | **What happens** |
| --- | --- |
| New File icon in the Explorer, type marks.py | Creates a Python file; .py tells VS Code it is Python |
| Click the Python version in the Status Bar | Shows the interpreters you can choose |
| Type the program, then Ctrl + S | Saves the program |
| python3 marks.py in the integrated terminal | Runs the program |
| The Run Python File button (▷) at the top right | Also runs the program, in the terminal |


### A real-world example

Geeta, a junior clerk at a college office in Belagavi, works out internal marks for 200 students each term using a calculator. She makes a small marks.py with a friend's help. Before trusting it, she tests it with three students whose totals she has already worked out by hand. Two match. The third is wrong, because she had typed m1 + m2 + m2. She fixes it, tests again, and only then uses it for the whole class.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The total is 8075 instead of 155 | input() gives text, so the text was joined | Wrap each input in int() |
| ValueError: invalid literal for int() | A word or a decimal was typed where a whole number was expected | Type digits only, such as 80; for decimals use float() |
| python3: can't open file 'marks.py' | The terminal is in a different folder, or the name is different | Run ls to check, and cd into the project folder |
| The program runs the old code | The file was not saved | Press Ctrl + S before running; a dot on the tab means unsaved changes |

# Reading 15: Debugging Applications


### What is it?

In Tutorial 8 you fixed errors by reading the message. Some bugs are harder: the program runs without any error but gives the wrong answer. AI programs often fail like this: a value in the wrong unit, an empty list, or a calculation that uses the wrong variable. To find such bugs, you need to see inside the program while it runs. That is what the **debugger** does.

The debugger pauses a program at a chosen line, so you can look at every variable at that moment. You tell it where to pause with a **breakpoint**: click just left of a line number and a red dot appears. When the program pauses, the line is highlighted in yellow. That line has **not** run yet.

In the tutorial's salary program, the debugger paused before the total was calculated. Changing basic from 30000 to 35000 with Set Value and clicking Step Over gave a new total of 55000. Then da was misspelt as daa, and stepping over showed a NameError on that line.


### Debugger tools at a glance


| **Do this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| Click left of a line number | Sets a breakpoint (red dot) where the program will pause |
| Run and Debug → Python Debugger → Python File | Starts the program in the debugger |
| Variables panel (left side) | Shows every variable and its current value |
| Debug Console (bottom panel) | Lets you type an expression, such as basic + hra + da, and see its value |
| Right-click a variable → Set Value | Changes a value to test "what if", without editing the code |
| Step Over (debug toolbar) | Runs the yellow line and pauses at the next one |
| Continue (debug toolbar) | Runs to the next breakpoint or to the end |
| Problems tab (bottom panel) | Lists the errors VS Code has found in your files |


### A real-world example

Joseph keeps the accounts of a small church in Kottayam and has written a Python program to total the monthly donations. The program runs, but its total is Rs 2,000 more than his notebook. He sets a breakpoint on the total line and starts the debugger. In the Variables panel he sees that one month's donation is 2500, not 500. He had typed an extra 2 in the data. The code was right; the input was wrong. He fixes it and the totals match.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The program runs to the end and never pauses | No breakpoint was set, or it is on a line after the error | Set the breakpoint on or before the line you want to check |
| The debugger stops with an error before the breakpoint | The error is on an earlier line | Read the highlighted line and the message, fix it, and start again |
| Run and Debug asks for a configuration | VS Code needs to know how to run the file | Choose Python Debugger, then Python File |
| A value you changed with Set Value is back to the old one next time | Set Value changes only this run, not the code | Edit the code if the change should stay |

# Reading 16: Git and Version Control


### What is it?

Most of us have a folder with files like report_final.docx, report_final2.docx and report_REALLY_final.docx. **Version control** solves this properly. Instead of making copies, you save snapshots of the whole project, each with a short note. You can see what changed, when and why, and go back to any snapshot. If a change makes results worse, you can see exactly what changed.

**Git** is the most widely used version control tool. It is free and runs on your own computer. It was created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds, who also created Linux. Almost every software and AI team in the world uses it.

Git works in three places. Your **working folder** holds your files as you edit them. git add puts the changes you choose into the **staging area**. git commit saves everything in the staging area as a snapshot in the **repository**, which Git keeps in a hidden .git folder.


### Commands at a glance


| **Type this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| sudo apt install git | Installs Git |
| git config --global user.name "Your Name" | Sets the name shown on your commits (once per computer) |
| git config --global user.email "you@example.com" | Sets the email shown on your commits (once per computer) |
| git init | Starts tracking the current folder; creates the hidden .git folder |
| git status | Shows which files have changed and which are staged |
| git add . | Stages every changed file in the folder (the dot means "everything here") |
| git commit -m "Add average calculation" | Saves the staged changes as a snapshot, with a message |
| git log --oneline | Lists your commits, newest first, one line each |

A good commit message says what the change does, in a few words: "Add average calculation" or "Fix spelling of Science column". Messages like "changes" or "update" tell you nothing months later.


### A real-world example

Shreya and two classmates in Guwahati are working on a final-year project. One evening, a change breaks the program a day before their review. Nobody can remember what the working version looked like. For the next project, Shreya runs git init on the first day and commits after every working step, with messages like "Add login page" and "Fix date format". When something breaks again, git log shows the last working commit, and they compare it with the broken code in minutes.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fatal: not a git repository | git init was not run in this folder, or you are in another folder | Run pwd to check where you are, then cd into the project or run git init |
| Author identity unknown, please tell me who you are | The name and email are not set | Run the two git config commands, then commit again |
| nothing added to commit but untracked files present | The files were not staged | Run git add . before git commit |
| A changed file is not in the commit | It was changed after git add | Run git add . again, then commit |

# Reading 17: Multiple Files and Refactoring


### What is it?

As a program grows, keeping everything in one file makes it hard to read and change. The answer is to split it into several files, each with one job. Real AI projects are split this way: one file loads data, another cleans it, another trains the model, another shows results. Each .py file is called a **module**, and code in one module can use what is defined in another with import.

In the tutorial, a Library folder held an empty file called `__init__.py`, which tells Python to treat the folder as a package, and four other files. books.py defined library_name = "Central Library". The other three files imported it and printed it:


```python
from books import library_name
print(library_name)
```

This means: from the module books (the file books.py), bring in library_name. The value is defined once, in one place, and used everywhere else.

**Refactoring** means improving the structure or names in code without changing what it does. Renaming a variable that is used in four files by hand is slow and easy to get wrong. VS Code's **Rename Symbol** changes the name everywhere it is used, in every file, in one step. It is smarter than find-and-replace: it changes only that variable, not the same letters inside other words.


### Commands at a glance


| **Type this or do this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| from books import library_name | Brings library_name from books.py into the current file |
| import books, then books.library_name | Brings in the whole module and uses its name with a dot |
| Search icon in the Activity Bar | Finds every place a word appears in the project |
| Cursor on a name, then F2 | Renames the symbol everywhere it is used (Rename Symbol) |
| File → Save All | Saves every changed file |


### A real-world example

Anand is building a small program for his father's medical shop in Madurai. All 300 lines are in one file, and whenever he changes the bill calculation, something in the stock list breaks. He splits it into stock.py, billing.py and main.py. The GST rate is now defined once, in billing.py, and imported where needed. When he decides that a variable called rate should be called gst_rate, he presses F2, types the new name and checks the three files. Every use has changed, and the program still runs.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'books' | The terminal is in a different folder from books.py | cd into the project folder, then run the file again |
| ImportError: cannot import name 'library_name' | The name is spelt differently in books.py, or books.py was not saved | Check the spelling, then save all files |
| The program prints an old value | A changed file was not saved | Use File → Save All, then run again |
| After find-and-replace, other words have changed too | Find-and-replace changes every match, even inside other words | Use F2 Rename Symbol for variable names |

# Reading 18: Connecting a Project to GitHub


### What is it?

Git keeps the history of your project on your own computer. **GitHub** is a website that keeps a copy of that repository online. Git is the tool; GitHub is one place to store and share what Git tracks. The online copy is called the **remote**.

With your project on GitHub, it is backed up, others can see it or work on it with you, and it becomes part of your public profile. Many employers look at GitHub profiles when hiring for data and AI roles. Most open source AI tools, including many used in this course, are developed and shared on GitHub.

To connect a project: sign up at github.com, create a new repository (keep it Public), and copy the commands GitHub shows under "...or create a new repository on the command line" into the VS Code terminal. The first time you push, VS Code asks you to sign in to GitHub in the browser. Allow it and authorise Visual Studio Code. After that, the daily routine is three commands: git add, git commit, git push.


### Commands at a glance


| **Type this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| git branch -M main | Names your main line of work "main", as GitHub expects |
| git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/StudentApp.git | Links your folder to the GitHub repository |
| git push -u origin main | Sends your commits to GitHub for the first time |
| git push | Sends new commits after the first time |
| git remote -v | Shows which GitHub repository the folder is linked to |


### A real-world example

Pooja, a B.Sc. student in Dehradun, applies for a data analyst internship. The form asks for a GitHub link. She has done several projects, but they are all on her laptop. She creates a GitHub account, pushes her two best projects and writes a short README for each, saying what it does and how to run it. In the interview, the manager opens one of them on his screen and asks her to walk him through it. She knows every line, because she wrote and committed each one.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| error: remote origin already exists | The folder is already linked to a repository | Check with git remote -v; use git remote set-url origin <url> to change it |
| error: src refspec main does not match any | There are no commits yet, or the branch is not called main | Make a commit first, then run git branch -M main |
| Your change is not on GitHub | You committed but did not push | Run git push, then refresh the GitHub page |
| A file with personal details is now public | It was committed and pushed | Keep such files out of the project from the start; ask on the forum how to remove it from the history |

# Reading 19: Building a Student Result System


### What is it?

This tutorial brings Modules 3 and 4 together in one complete program: a menu in the terminal that registers students, records their marks, works out grades and prints a report card. The project was started entirely from the terminal, and code . opened the folder in VS Code. The dot means "this folder".

The program is built from **functions**: named blocks of code that each do one job. You create a function with def and run it by calling its name. The student records are kept in a **dictionary**, which stores each student's details under their ID, the way a register lists each student under a roll number.

When an ID that was never registered is entered, the program prints "Student not found" instead of crashing. Checking for wrong input like this is called **input validation**, and it makes a program reliable for real users. The same pattern (store data, process it, show results, and loop on the user's choices) is at the heart of almost every application, including AI chatbots.


### The program at a glance


| **Part of the program** | **Its job** |
| --- | --- |
| students_db | A dictionary holding every student's name and marks, looked up by ID |
| register_student() | Asks for an ID and name, and adds the student |
| enter_marks() | Asks for an ID, a subject and marks, and stores them for that student |
| calculate_grade() | Turns marks into a grade: A, B, C or F |
| display_result() | Prints a neat report card for one student |
| main_menu() | Shows options 1–4 in a loop, calls the right function, and exits on 4 |


### Commands at a glance


| **Type this** | **What it does** |
| --- | --- |
| mkdir ~/Desktop/StudentResultSystem | Creates the project folder on the Desktop |
| cd ~/Desktop/StudentResultSystem | Moves into it |
| code . | Opens the current folder in VS Code |
| python3 main.py | Runs the program |


### A real-world example

Mr Bhattacharya teaches at a coaching centre in Siliguri. Each month he writes report cards for 60 students by hand. A former student, now studying computer applications, builds him a menu program like this one. The first version crashes whenever he types a roll number that does not exist. She adds a check that prints "Student not found" and returns to the menu. She also tests a student who scored exactly on a grade boundary, to make sure the grade is right. He now prints all 60 report cards in an afternoon.


### Common mistakes


| **What you see** | **Why it happens** | **How to fix it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| KeyError: 102 | The program looked up an ID that is not in the dictionary | Check with if student_id in students_db before looking it up |

assessments.title: Class Results Analyser
assessments.instructions_markdown:
You are helping a college department look at a class's test results. Your job is to explore the marks in Jupyter, turn your steps into a program in VS Code that a teacher can use, keep the project's history with Git, and share it on GitHub.

#### The data


Create a file called class-marks.csv with these lines. The names are made up. Each mark is out of 100.


The grades are worked out from each student's average mark:


| **Average** | **Grade** |
| --- | --- |
| 75 or more | A |
| 60 to less than 75 | B |
| 40 to less than 60 | C |
| Less than 40 | F |


#### What to do


#### Step 1. Set up the project (Modules 2 and 4)


1. Create a folder called class-results, with the folders notebooks, datasets, images and outputs inside it.

2. Save class-marks.csv in datasets.

3. Open the folder in VS Code and run git init. Make your first commit, with the message "Add class marks data".

#### Step 2. Explore the marks in Jupyter (Modules 1 and 2)


In notebooks, create 01_explore_marks.ipynb and do the following. Explain each step in a Markdown cell before the code.

1. Load the CSV with Pandas and show head(), shape and info().

2. Add a Total column and an Average column:

```python
data["Total"] = data["Maths"] + data["Science"] + data["English"]
data["Average"] = data["Total"] / 3
```

1. Find the class topper (the student with the highest Total), the average mark in each subject, and how many students have an Average of 60 or more.

2. Draw two labelled graphs and save them in images: a bar chart of the average mark in each subject, and a bar chart of each student's Total.

3. End with a Markdown cell of two or three sentences on what you found.

4. Use Restart Kernel and Run All Cells, then export the notebook as HTML or PDF into outputs.

#### Step 3. Build the program in VS Code (Module 3 and Tutorials 17 and 19)


Write a program in two files:

* results.py, with a function grade(average) that returns A, B, C or F using the table above, and a function that reads class-marks.csv.

* main.py, with a menu in a loop: 1. Show one student's result, 2. Show the class summary, 3. Exit.

Option 1 asks for a name and prints that student's marks, total, average (rounded to 2 decimals) and grade. If the name is not in the file, it prints "Student not found" and returns to the menu. Option 2 prints the number of students, the class topper, and how many students got each grade.

Commit when the program works, with a clear message.

#### Step 4. Check it with the debugger (Tutorial 15)


Set a breakpoint inside grade() and run the program in the debugger for Gauri. Use the Variables panel to check her average and the grade returned. Note in your README what you checked and what you saw.

#### Step 5. Share it on GitHub (Tutorials 16 and 18)


1. Write a README.md with the project's name, one or two lines on what it does, how to run main.py, and your debugger check from Step 4.

2. Commit, then create a public repository named class-results on GitHub, connect your folder and push.

3. Open the repository link in a private browser window to check that anyone can see it.

#### What to submit on Spoken Social


1. The link to your GitHub repository.

2. The output of git log --oneline, pasted as text. There should be at least three commits.

3. The program's output for: Gauri, a name that is not in the file, and the class summary, pasted as text.

4. The topper, the three subject averages and your two graphs (screenshots) from the notebook.

5. A short note of **200–300 words** in your own words. Explain what you did in each step, why you would use Jupyter for some parts and VS Code for others, and describe one problem you met and how you solved it.

Do not include any password or personal details in your submission or your repository.

#### How the capstone is marked


Evaluators use this marking guide. The 10 points are scaled to the 5% of course marks for the capstone.


| **Part** | **What the evaluator checks** | **Points** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project set-up | class-results has the four folders, with the files in the right places | 1 |
| Notebook | Loads the data, adds Total and Average, finds the topper, subject averages and count of 60 or more; Markdown before each step; runs from the top | 2 |
| Graphs | Two bar charts, each with a title and axis labels, saved in images | 1 |
| Program | Two files; the result for one student and the class summary are correct; grade() follows the table | 2 |
| Input validation | A name not in the file gives "Student not found", and the menu continues | 1 |
| Git and GitHub | Public repository with at least three commits with clear messages, and a README that says how to run the program | 2 |
| Written note | 200–300 words, in your own words, covers the steps, Jupyter versus VS Code, and one problem solved | 1 |
| **Total** |  | **10** |


*Expected results, for the evaluator: Ishita is the topper (Total 276, Average 92.0). Subject averages: Maths 67.3, Science 67.95, English 70.35. 14 students have an Average of 60 or more. Gauri: Total 192, Average 64.0, Grade B. Grade counts: A 8, B 6, C 5, F 1 (Jagdish, Average 39.67).*

#### Tips


* Build the notebook one step at a time. Run each cell and check the output before writing the next one.

* You can use Pandas in results.py to read the CSV. If the import fails in VS Code, click the Python version in the Status Bar and choose the interpreter from your virtual environment (Tutorial 14).

* In main.py, get option 1 working for one student before you write the menu loop.

* Test grade() on the boundaries: an average of exactly 75, 60 and 40 should give A, B and C.

* Commit each time something works. If a later change breaks the program, git log shows you the last working version.

* Your note matters. Evaluators want to see that you understand what each part does, not just that it runs.
